anomaly_def.Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions and rollback records accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating on-disk and in-memory footprints and lengthening visibility checks.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Sessions repeatedly serialize on hot buffer pages, latches, and I/O slots, stalling while trying to pin, read, or flush shared pages.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes drive host CPU utilization to sustained saturation, starving other work and enlarging run-queue and scheduler waits.

When these three conditions coexist, the system exhibits a feedback loop of stress signals: rapidly growing table and index sizes inflate the working-set beyond the buffer pool, causing constant page evictions and refills. Hot root pages and version chains become latch hot-spots, producing surges of buffer-busy and latch waits. Spin-loop retries and repeated visibility checks consume CPU, pushing host utilization to the ceiling. Checkpoint and background-writer processes fight for CPU and I/O, while cleanup workers fall further behind, seen as ever-rising dead-tuple ratios, lengthening autovacuum runtimes, and warnings about transaction-ID or UNDO wraparound. Application queries experience both CPU-bound queuing delays and IO-induced latency spikes, making performance unpredictable and hard to attribute to a single layer.

Causally, heavy update/delete churn triggers MVCC bloat; the swollen relation footprint overwhelms an already tight buffer pool, amplifying buffer churn and latch contention. Each failed latch acquisition can induce spin-waiting, directly inflating CPU demand. As CPUs saturate, background cleaners and checkpointers lose scheduling opportunities, slowing version reclamation and dirty-page flushing. The slower cleanup further escalates bloat, which in turn increases buffer pressure and contention, closing a vicious cycle that degrades throughput and threatens outages from transaction-horizon or space-exhaustion limits.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the number of TCP keepalive messages that can be lost before the server connection to the client is considered dead.
entry.trigger_condition: The number of lost TCP keepalive probes reaches tcp_keepalives_count on systems supporting TCP_KEEPCNT.
entry.workload_impact: The server can consider the client connection dead after the configured keepalive failure threshold.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
